title: Surface charges in a Rydberg atom-nanowaveguide hybrid quantum system
authors: Aswathy Raj, Anna Kortel, Krishna Jadeja, Dylan J. Brown, Alexey Vylegzhanin, Robert Löw, Síle Nic Chormaic
abstract: Hybrid quantum platforms based on highly excited Rydberg atoms coupled to nanophotonics devices offer a promising route toward scalable quantum networks and integrated quantum technologies. However, the close proximity of Rydberg atoms to dielectric nanostructures makes these systems particularly susceptible to uncontrolled surface electric fields that can lead to a degradation of the excitation process. Here, we experimentally investigate Rydberg excitation of laser-cooled $^{87}$Rb atoms via the evanescent field of an optical nanofiber in the presence of fiber-guided red- and blue-detuned light fields as used to trap ground state atoms in fiber-based dipole traps. We observe a time evolution of the Rydberg excitation spectrum when both the dipole trapping fields are on and the additional spectral features that appear can be suppressed by applying an external oscillating electric field to the system, strongly indicating that surface charge accumulation is responsible for the observed spectral feature. The experimental results are reproduced qualitatively by a model that incorporates DC energy level shifts arising from electric fields generated by charges deposited on the nanofiber surface. We identify Rydberg-ground state collisional ionization, which is enhanced by the dipole trapping fields, as the dominant mechanism for charge generation. These results provide new insight into charge dynamics at dielectric nanophotonic interfaces and establish practical guidelines for mitigating surface charge-induced electric fields in fiber-integrated Rydberg quantum systems.
summary: The paper experimentally investigates how surface charge accumulation on optical nanofibers degrades Rydberg excitation in trapped atoms. By observing time-dependent spectral shifts and suppressing them with an external AC field, the authors confirm that surface charges are the culprit. This work establishes crucial guidelines for mitigating these environmental electric fields in future integrated quantum technologies.
main_problem: The study investigates how uncontrolled surface electric fields, arising from charge accumulation on dielectric nanostructures, degrade Rydberg excitation processes in hybrid quantum systems.
main_result: Spectral deformations observed during Rydberg excitation are strongly attributed to DC energy level shifts caused by accumulated surface charges. Applying an external oscillating electric field successfully suppresses these spectral features.
method: The research combines experimental measurements of time-evolving Rydberg spectra with theoretical modeling using the Lindblad master equation to simulate charge effects.
model_or_system: The system involves laser-cooled $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms excited into high-$n$ Rydberg states near an optical nanofiber (ONF). The model incorporates DC energy level shifts ($\delta_{DC}$) derived from surface charges and uses the Lindblad master equation to track population dynamics.
key_observables: Time evolution of the Rydberg excitation spectrum, spectral splitting/deformation magnitude, and remaining MOT population ($N'$).
important_parameters: Rydberg state ($n	ext{D}_{5/2}$), trapping beam wavelengths (762 nm, 1064 nm), external AC field frequency (100 kHz), and surface charge density.
main_assumptions: The dominant mechanism for charge generation is identified as Rydberg-ground state collisional ionization enhanced by dipole trapping fields. The model assumes the ONF is single-mode at relevant wavelengths.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic setups, excitation schemes, time evolution of spectra showing deformation, and comparisons between spectra with and without external AC field suppression.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the experimental setup and observing spectral anomalies under trapping fields. It then uses external fields to diagnose charge effects, models these shifts theoretically, and finally identifies collisional ionization as the source of the charges, providing mitigation guidelines.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant for AMO physicists working on open quantum systems because it provides a concrete, experimentally validated mechanism (surface charging) that limits the scalability of integrated Rydberg quantum devices, offering practical engineering solutions.
